paras: The Eastman camp meeting riot took place on Sunday, August 6, 1882, at Eastman, Dodge County, Georgia, when the town marshal's party shot dead a Black prisoner fleeing arrest and a crowd of Black excursionists then killed a young white man, James Q. Harvard, whom they took for one of the officers. Two accounts add that armed white citizens then killed three Black men in a clash with the crowd. Twenty-two Black defendants were convicted of Harvard's murder, five were hanged together at Eastman in October, and the two officers were indicted for manslaughter.

Circulars had advertised a Black camp meeting at Eastman with reduced railroad excursion rates, and the Omaha special quoted a promise of 'more amusement' than at any camp meeting in Georgia. About 11 o'clock that Sunday two crowded excursion trains arrived from Macon and Hawkinsville and from Jesup, and a later local account put the visitors at two or three thousand. White accounts dwelt on whisky, gambling and weapons among the crowd.

According to the Macon Telegraph's Eastman correspondent, a Black man reported that another had stolen his watch, and Marshal J. B. A. Buchan and his assistant, Pete Harrell, arrested the accused man; he broke loose on the way to jail and was shot dead. The Omaha Bee's Atlanta special named him Jake Johnson, 'a notorious colored gambler', and said the marshal fired after Johnson knocked the deputy down, while the New York Sun later wrote that both officers fired and the deputy's shot killed him. Other papers called him Jake Tarropy, Tarrapy or Terrapin.

His body was carried to the platform before Sheriff Sapp's store, where a crowd gathered calling for revenge, and Sapp left town under threat. The local retrospective says the crowd caught deputy Harrell near the post office and cut him, then let him go when its attention was turned to Harvard, a young man from Cochran who had come on the excursion. The crowd chased Harvard several hundred yards with shots and missiles to the house of W. W. Harrell on Fifth Avenue, where he hid under the house.

Some two or three hundred people surrounded the premises, tore down the fence and palings, fired into the house and threatened to burn it, while W. W. Harrell and his grandson held the gate. When Harrell agreed to let five men search, the crowd entered, found Harvard and dragged him out over the pleas of Jordan Smith, a Black man who said he had known him all his life. One of the crowd shot Harvard in the head and others beat him with sticks by the gate; the retrospective said no witness could identify the shooter.

According to the Omaha special and the New York Sun, the crowd then went into town looking for the marshal and met armed citizens, and in the exchange of fire three Black men were killed and several people wounded on both sides. The detailed Eastman accounts describe no such clash and say the crowd quieted down and left on the five o'clock train.

Arrests began that evening, and by August 12 twenty-two prisoners had been committed, with volunteers from Cochran helping and a volunteer guard posted at the jail against 'mob violence'. The Omaha special reported that lynching of the rioters was feared. Eastman and Hawkinsville citizens passed resolutions against Sunday excursion trains.

At a special term of Dodge Superior Court one bill charged twenty-six Black defendants with Harvard's murder, and three batch trials ended in twenty-two convictions. Judge Pate sentenced six to death, and the grand jury also returned manslaughter bills against Buchan and A. P. Harrell, whose outcome does not appear in the coverage. A penitentiary guard said twelve armed men waited near Eastman to fire on the convicts' train because not all had been sentenced to hang.

After Governor Colquitt reviewed the record, Isaac Shipman was reprieved, and on October 20 Ella Moore, Joe King, Simon O'Quinn, Bob Donelson and Reddick Powell were hanged at Eastman under a large armed guard. Shipman's sentence was commuted to life imprisonment on October 27.

The first Macon wire ran on August 7 and 8 in papers from Washington to Yankton, calling Harvard an 'innocent white man' killed by mistake, and the Savannah Morning News headed it 'MURDERED BY A MOB'. An Atlanta special followed under headlines such as 'BLOODTHIRSTY BLACKS' and 'BLOOD-THIRSTY MOKES', while a short brief giving three white and two Black dead circulated in weeklies into mid-August. None of these reports questioned the officers' shooting of the prisoner.

The Savannah Morning News followed the case closely through its Eastman correspondent, who rebutted the Atlanta Post-Appeal's claim that the whites' 'drawing of the color line' caused the trouble. Its editorial on the hanging said the crime would have justified the citizens of Eastman in lynching the rioters on the spot, and praised them for leaving the case to the courts. A defense counsel's account in the same paper described the Atlanta Defiance and Savannah Echo, papers it called Black-published, as attacking the convictions of 'innocent colored men by the wholesale'. The Weekly Defiance credited W. A. Pledger, E. Seward Small and Capt. Pleasant with bringing the reprieve before the governor and said all the condemned should have been spared.

Accounts differ on who shot the prisoner: the Macon wire and the Sun named the deputy, the Omaha special the marshal, and the Atlanta wire both officers. They also differ on how Harvard was singled out, with the Eastman correspondent repeating that deputy Harrell pointed him out, a penitentiary guard naming the marshal, and other accounts saying the crowd simply chased a white man it saw running. The death toll ranges from Harvard and Johnson alone in the local narratives to five dead in the Omaha and Sun accounts, while one Atlanta brief gave three white and two Black dead.

reader.title: Eastman camp meeting riot
bases: The anti-Black killing every account reports is the town marshal's or deputy's fatal shooting of a fleeing Black prisoner (A2, A17, A20, A60); the riot that followed was a Black crowd's killing of a white man (A17, A57), and two accounts add that armed white citizens then killed three Black men (A20, A60).

The Macon wire, the Atlanta special, the local Macon Telegraph correspondent and the later Eastman retrospective independently agree on the prisoner's shooting and Harvard's killing (A2, A16, A17, A20, A57), though the armed clash with citizens rests on two accounts only (A20, A60).

accounts.gist: A deputy marshal shot a fleeing prisoner, Jake Tarropy; the crowd chased the deputy into a house and killed an innocent white man there, mistaking him for the deputy.

accounts.gist: Buchan and Harrell arrested a man accused of stealing a watch; he was shot while escaping; it 'is said' Harrell told the crowd he was not Harrell and pointed to Harvard, who was hunted into W. W. Harrell's house and killed.

accounts.label: Atlanta special to the Omaha Bee
accounts.gist: The marshal shot Jake Johnson after he knocked the deputy down; the crowd killed Harvard; armed citizens then killed three Black men; lynching of the rioters was feared.

accounts.label: Penitentiary guard Turner
accounts.gist: The marshal shot the escaping prisoner and, it was said, pointed out Harvard as the man who had killed him.

accounts.label: Defense counsel Jack Brown
accounts.gist: The prisoner was killed trying to escape about 2 p.m.; hundreds pursued a young man they took for the marshal and killed him; the trials were fair.

accounts.label: Eastman retrospective at the hanging
accounts.gist: The crowd caught and cut deputy Harrell, then was somehow led to take Harvard for the marshal, besieged the Harrell house for half an hour, and shot and beat him; no witness could identify the shooter.

accounts.label: New York Sun at the hanging
accounts.gist: The deputy, Peter Harrell, fired the fatal shot at Johnson; after killing Harvard the crowd met armed citizens and lost three men.

framing.detail: Wire and Georgia headlines blamed the crowd: 'MURDERED BY A MOB. Infurlated Negroes Kill a White Man by Mistake', 'BLOODTHIRSTY BLACKS', 'BLOOD-THIRSTY MOKES'.
The Savannah Morning News endorsed the five hangings and said the crime would have justified lynch law, praising Eastman for letting the courts act.
The Atlanta Post-Appeal, as summarized by an Eastman correspondent, blamed the whites' 'drawing of the color line'; the correspondent rebutted it.
The Weekly Defiance, an Atlanta paper described in Savannah as Black-published, said all the condemned should have been reprieved.

conflicts.note: Possibly a real name and a nickname; the papers do not reconcile them.
The local correspondent says only that he 'was shot at and killed' (A17); both officers were later indicted for manslaughter (A56).
